primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Adequate folate before conception and during early pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube closure defects that arise in the first month of development.
vignette: A 27-year-old woman planning pregnancy asks which nutrient is most important to begin before conception to reduce the risk of spina bifida in a future fetus.
distractor_notes: Vitamin B12 is important for DNA synthesis but folic acid is the established preventive supplement for most neural tube defects.
Vitamin C deficiency does not cause neural tube closure failure.
Vitamin K prevents bleeding disorders and is unrelated to neural tube closure.
Excess vitamin A can itself be teratogenic and is not used to prevent neural tube defects.
key_expl: Periconceptional folic acid supplementation substantially reduces the risk of neural tube defects.
objective: Identify folic acid as the key preventive nutrient for neural tube defects.

sources.title: Neural Tube Defects
sources.support: MedlinePlus states that enough folic acid before and during pregnancy prevents most neural tube defects.

sources.title: Folic Acid
sources.support: CDC recommends folic acid before and during early pregnancy to help prevent neural tube defects.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: The fetal ductus arteriosus shunts blood from pulmonary artery to aorta; after birth rising oxygen tension and falling prostaglandins promote closure.
vignette: A premature infant has a continuous machine-like murmur. Echocardiography shows persistent flow between the pulmonary artery and descending aorta.
lead: Which fetal structure failed to close?
distractor_notes: The foramen ovale connects the atria, not the pulmonary artery to aorta.
The ductus venosus bypasses the fetal liver.
The umbilical vein carries oxygenated placental blood to the fetus and does not connect pulmonary artery to aorta.
The aortic isthmus is part of the aorta and is not a fetal shunt vessel.
key_expl: Patent ductus arteriosus is persistence of the fetal vascular connection between pulmonary artery and aorta.
objective: Identify the ductus arteriosus from its fetal circulatory connection and postnatal PDA findings.
clues: continuous murmur with pulmonary artery-to-aorta flow

sources.title: Patent ductus arteriosus
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes the ductus arteriosus as a fetal vessel connecting the pulmonary artery and aorta that normally closes after birth.

sources.title: Patent Ductus Arteriosus
sources.support: CDC describes PDA as persistence of the fetal ductus arteriosus after birth.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Autoantibodies target platelet antigens, accelerating splenic platelet clearance and causing isolated thrombocytopenia with mucocutaneous bleeding.
vignette: A 7-year-old child develops petechiae and easy bruising 2 weeks after a viral illness. Hemoglobin and leukocyte counts are normal, but platelet count is 18,000/µL.
distractor_notes: TTP usually includes microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and systemic organ injury rather than isolated thrombocytopenia.
DIC causes consumptive coagulopathy with abnormal coagulation studies and systemic illness.
Aplastic anemia causes pancytopenia rather than isolated thrombocytopenia.
Hemophilia A causes deep-tissue bleeding with a normal platelet count.
key_expl: Postviral isolated severe thrombocytopenia with petechiae in a child is classic immune thrombocytopenia.
objective: Recognize immune thrombocytopenia from isolated platelet loss and mucocutaneous bleeding.

sources.title: Immune thrombocytopenia
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes immune platelet destruction causing thrombocytopenia, petechiae, and bruising.

sources.title: Platelet Disorders
sources.support: NHLBI describes immune thrombocytopenia as immune destruction of platelets causing bleeding manifestations.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency permits unusually large von Willebrand factor multimers to persist, promoting platelet-rich microthrombi and microangiopathic hemolysis.
vignette: A 36-year-old woman has confusion, fever, thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, elevated LDH, and mildly impaired renal function.
lead: Deficiency of which enzyme best explains this disorder?
distractor_notes: Factor VIII deficiency causes hemophilia A and does not cause microangiopathic hemolysis.
Protein C deficiency causes thrombophilia rather than thrombocytopenic microangiopathy.
G6PD deficiency causes oxidant hemolysis without platelet-rich microthrombi.
Myeloperoxidase deficiency affects microbial killing and is unrelated to TTP.
key_expl: TTP is strongly associated with severe deficiency of ADAMTS13, the protease that cleaves ultra-large vWF multimers.
objective: Link TTP to severe ADAMTS13 deficiency.

sources.title: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
sources.support: MedlinePlus identifies ADAMTS13 deficiency as the central enzymatic abnormality in TTP.

sources.title: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes ADAMTS13-related failure to control vWF-mediated platelet clumping.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Systemic coagulation activation generates diffuse microthrombi while consuming platelets and clotting factors, producing simultaneous thrombosis and bleeding.
vignette: A patient with septic shock develops oozing from venipuncture sites, thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, and elevated D-dimer.
distractor_notes: ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia with normal coagulation tests.
Hemophilia A causes isolated intrinsic-pathway impairment, not low fibrinogen and elevated D-dimer from consumption.
Von Willebrand disease causes inherited mucocutaneous bleeding, not acute systemic factor consumption in sepsis.
Factor V Leiden causes thrombosis without consumptive bleeding and low fibrinogen.
key_expl: Sepsis plus consumptive thrombocytopenia, prolonged coagulation times, low fibrinogen, and elevated D-dimer is classic DIC.
objective: Recognize disseminated intravascular coagulation from systemic consumption of platelets and clotting factors.
clues: bleeding plus low fibrinogen and high D-dimer

sources.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes pathologic systemic coagulation activation with microthrombi and consumption of clotting proteins causing bleeding.

sources.title: Blood Clotting Disorders
sources.support: NHLBI describes DIC as widespread abnormal clotting with consumption of clotting factors and bleeding risk.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Factor V Leiden is resistant to inactivation by activated protein C, prolonging procoagulant factor V activity and increasing venous thrombosis risk.
vignette: A 29-year-old woman develops a deep venous thrombosis after starting estrogen-containing contraception. Her father had recurrent venous thromboses. Testing identifies factor V Leiden.
lead: Which regulatory defect most directly causes the thrombophilia?
correct: Resistance of factor V to activated protein C
distractors: Failure of antithrombin to inhibit thrombin
Failure of platelets to bind von Willebrand factor
distractor_notes: Antithrombin deficiency is a separate inherited thrombophilia.
Tissue factor deficiency would impair coagulation rather than promote thrombosis.
Excess fibrinogen degradation would promote bleeding, not inherited venous thrombosis.
Defective platelet-vWF interaction causes bleeding disorders such as Bernard-Soulier syndrome.
key_expl: The factor V Leiden variant makes factor V resistant to activated protein C-mediated inactivation.
objective: Explain factor V Leiden thrombophilia through activated protein C resistance.

sources.title: Factor V Leiden thrombophilia
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics states that factor V Leiden cannot be inactivated normally by activated protein C.

sources.title: F5 gene
sources.support: F5 encodes coagulation factor V; the Leiden variant causes activated protein C resistance.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Activated protein C normally limits coagulation by inactivating factors Va and VIIIa; deficiency therefore increases venous thrombosis risk.
vignette: A 24-year-old man has recurrent deep venous thromboses and a family history of similar events. Testing shows low functional protein C activity.
lead: Which clotting factors are normally inactivated by activated protein C?
distractor_notes: Antithrombin is the major inhibitor of thrombin and factor Xa.
Tissue factor pathway inhibitor regulates tissue factor–VIIa signaling.
Protein C does not primarily inactivate XIa and XIIa.
Protein C is not a direct fibrinogen or factor XIII protease.
key_expl: Activated protein C, with protein S as a cofactor, inactivates factors Va and VIIIa.
objective: Identify the anticoagulant targets of activated protein C.

sources.title: Protein C deficiency
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes protein C as an anticoagulant protein that inactivates procoagulant factors.

sources.title: Congenital protein C or S deficiency
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes protein C deficiency as an inherited disorder causing abnormal blood clotting.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: An acquired PIGA mutation prevents GPI-anchor synthesis, causing loss of complement-regulatory proteins such as CD55 and CD59 and intravascular hemolysis.
vignette: A 34-year-old man has episodic dark urine, fatigue, abdominal pain, and an unusual hepatic-vein thrombosis. Flow cytometry shows absent CD55 and CD59 on blood cells.
lead: Which molecular defect best explains these findings?
distractors: Loss of spectrin from the erythrocyte cytoskeleton
distractor_notes: Spectrin defects cause hereditary spherocytosis, not loss of CD55/CD59.
Heme oxygenase is unrelated to GPI anchoring and complement protection.
Beta-globin deficiency causes beta-thalassemia.
Platelet glycoprotein autoantibodies cause immune thrombocytopenia rather than complement-mediated hemolysis.
key_expl: PIGA loss prevents GPI-anchored complement regulators from attaching to blood-cell membranes, allowing complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis.
objective: Explain PNH through acquired PIGA mutation and loss of GPI-anchored complement regulators.
clues: dark urine and unusual venous thrombosis

sources.title: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes acquired PIGA mutations and loss of GPI-anchored complement-protective proteins in PNH.

sources.title: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
sources.support: MedlinePlus explains that PIG-A loss prevents protective proteins from attaching to blood cells, allowing complement-mediated destruction.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Failure or immune destruction of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells causes hypocellular marrow and pancytopenia without marrow infiltration.
vignette: A 32-year-old woman has fatigue, recurrent infections, and easy bruising. CBC shows anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow biopsy is markedly hypocellular with fatty replacement.
distractor_notes: Acute leukemia usually shows marrow replacement by blasts rather than hypocellular fatty marrow.
Iron deficiency causes isolated anemia rather than pancytopenia.
ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia.
Polycythemia vera is a myeloproliferative disorder with increased cell production.
key_expl: Pancytopenia with a markedly hypocellular fatty marrow is diagnostic of aplastic anemia.
objective: Recognize aplastic anemia from pancytopenia and hypocellular bone marrow.

sources.title: Aplastic anemia
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes aplastic anemia as bone marrow failure causing reduced production of red cells, white cells, and platelets.

sources.title: Aplastic Anemia
sources.support: NHLBI describes aplastic anemia as failure of bone marrow to make enough blood cells.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Folate deficiency impairs one-carbon transfer reactions needed for nucleotide synthesis, causing defective DNA replication and megaloblastic hematopoiesis without the neurologic injury typical of vitamin B12 deficiency.
vignette: A 48-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder has fatigue and macrocytosis. Hypersegmented neutrophils are present. Serum folate is low, and neurologic examination is normal.
lead: Which cellular process is most directly impaired?
correct: DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing hematopoietic precursors
distractor_notes: Heme synthesis defects cause sideroblastic or related anemias, not classic megaloblastic changes.
Fatty-acid beta-oxidation defects do not cause hypersegmented neutrophils.
Globin-chain translation defects cause thalassemias.
Iron absorption defects cause microcytic iron deficiency rather than macrocytosis.
key_expl: Folate is essential for nucleotide synthesis; deficiency impairs DNA replication and produces megaloblastic anemia.
objective: Explain folate-deficiency macrocytosis through defective DNA synthesis.
clues: low folate and no neurologic deficits

sources.title: Folate-deficiency anemia
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes folate deficiency as causing megaloblastic macrocytic anemia.

sources.title: Folate — Health Professional Fact Sheet
sources.support: NIH ODS describes folate as essential for one-carbon transfer and nucleic acid synthesis.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: The PML-RARA fusion from t(15;17) blocks myeloid differentiation at the promyelocyte stage and is specifically targetable with differentiation therapy.
vignette: A 34-year-old woman presents with bruising and DIC. Bone marrow shows abnormal promyelocytes with numerous Auer rods. Cytogenetics demonstrates t(15;17).
lead: Which fusion protein is most likely present?
distractor_notes: BCR-ABL1 is characteristic of CML and some ALL.
MYC-IGH is characteristic of Burkitt lymphoma.
ETV6-RUNX1 occurs in a subset of childhood ALL.
BCL2-IGH is characteristic of follicular lymphoma.
key_expl: APL is defined by PML-RARA, usually from t(15;17).
objective: Associate APL morphology and DIC with the PML-RARA fusion.

sources.title: Acute promyelocytic leukemia
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes APL as driven by the PML-RARA fusion from t(15;17).

sources.title: RARA gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes RARA rearrangement with PML in acute promyelocytic leukemia.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: The BCR-ABL1 fusion encodes a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that drives uncontrolled myeloid proliferation.
vignette: A 52-year-old man has fatigue, splenomegaly, leukocytosis with a full spectrum of granulocyte maturation, and a t(9;22) translocation.
lead: Which molecular abnormality is most likely driving this disease?
distractors: Loss of RB1 in retinal cells
MYC translocation to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain locus
distractor_notes: PML-RARA defines acute promyelocytic leukemia.
JAK2 mutations are common in polycythemia vera and other myeloproliferative neoplasms, but the Philadelphia chromosome specifically indicates BCR-ABL1.
RB1 loss causes retinoblastoma.
MYC-IGH is characteristic of Burkitt lymphoma.
key_expl: The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) produces BCR-ABL1, a constitutively active tyrosine kinase.
objective: Connect the Philadelphia chromosome with BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase activity in CML.

sources.title: Chronic myeloid leukemia
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes CML as driven by the BCR-ABL1 fusion from the Philadelphia chromosome.

sources.title: ABL1 gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes the constitutively active BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase in CML.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Deficiency of C5 through C9 impairs membrane attack complex formation and markedly increases susceptibility to recurrent invasive Neisseria infections.
vignette: A 19-year-old man has had two episodes of meningococcal meningitis despite appropriate vaccination. Quantitative immunoglobulins and neutrophil function are normal.
lead: Which immune defect is most likely?
correct: Deficiency of terminal complement components C5-C9
distractor_notes: BTK deficiency causes absent mature B cells and pan-hypogammaglobulinemia.
NADPH oxidase deficiency causes recurrent catalase-positive bacterial and fungal infections.
ADA deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency in infancy.
Selective IgA deficiency predisposes mainly to mucosal infections and does not specifically cause recurrent invasive Neisseria infection.
key_expl: The membrane attack complex formed by C5b-C9 is particularly important for killing Neisseria species.
objective: Associate recurrent invasive Neisseria infection with terminal complement deficiency.

sources.title: Complement Blood Test
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes complement as a group of proteins that helps destroy microbes.

sources.title: Complement Deficiencies
sources.support: NIAID describes terminal complement defects as predisposing to recurrent Neisseria infection.
